newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine peso teeters amid Asia currency turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Philippine peso teeters amid Asia currency turmoil.

text.p: The Philippine peso teetered on Thursday, buffeted by fresh turmoil in the region's currency markets and a sharp drop in domestic interest rates, economists and treasurers said.

The rate cut was not even enough to spark a revival in the stock market where the main index slumped to a 20-month low with foreign investors finding little to tempt them to bring their money back in the face of a continuing Southeast Asian currency crisis. The stock index ended down 1.33 percent at 2,493.49.
The Philippine peso fell 57 centavos to a low of 29.620 per dollar minutes after the market opened, down from the previous day's close of 29.050.
Its weakness was triggered by a four-percentage point cut in the central bank's closely watched overnight rate to 14 percent.
That is slightly above the 10 to 12 percent range before the peso came under persistent attack starting in April on fears that its economy was going down the same troubled path as Thailand's.
The overnight rate went up to a 2 1/2-year high of 32 percent at the height of the speculative attack, which finally forced the Philippine government last month to allow a devaluation of the peso.
Bank treasurers and economists welcomed the rate cut.
"The central bank is finally allowing market forces to dictate the movement of the peso, which is a good move," ING Bank economists Manuel Lim said.
The peso weakness was due to a normal rise in dollar requirements by importers who are getting ready for the Christmas season, he said.
And measures taken by the central bank following last month's peso crisis has effectively shut the door on speculators and helped neutralise any impact from fresh currency attacks in the region.
The central bank temporarily suspended non-deliverable forward dollar sales, pared down commercial banks' open dollar positions to five percent, and more than doubled their liquidity reserves.

"The foreign exchange market is very much driven by commercial demand. The market is on its own now ... This is a very normal trading day with a respectable volume," said Jaime Panganiban, treasurer of Bank of America.
Panganiban said exporters have started to unload their dollars given the high exchange rate, providing a natural floor to the peso fall.
The rate cut also depressed the interbank call loan rate to 14.09375 percent from 18.0625 percent. However, some banks were still defensive, lending overnight money as high as 16 percent.
"Some banks were initially unsure whether the rates will stay that low, given the peso volatility early in the day," one money market trader said.
However, Antonio Agcaoili, treasurer of Banco Santander Manila, said rates will eventually settle to a more normal level, enough to spur the real economy back to full throttle.
"The central bank's priority right now is to manage the interest rate. Keeping a higher interest rate to protect the currency might be damaging to the economy in the long term," he said.
The increase in banks' liquidity reserves should rein in inflationary pressure coming from peso depreciation and lower interest rate regime, Agcaoili added.
